extracted.intended_audience: students of theology, clergy, and readers of Christian doctrinal exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Defines and explains key biblical and doctrinal terms (Kingdom of God, holy/sacred, sacraments, Word of God, prophet) and sets criteria for interpreting prophecy and modes of divine speech. Presents scriptural examples and distinctions used to evaluate meanings and claims of revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom of God (proper meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdom of God is properly meant a Common-wealth, instituted (by the consent of those which were to be subject thereto) for their civil government, regulating behaviour towards God and one another; a real, not metaphoric, earthly kingdom in which God is King and the High Priest his viceroy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by scriptural citations (Exod., 1 Sam., Isaiah, Micah, Ezekiel, Luke, Acts). The text argues the Kingdom is a civil polity (not merely spiritual), restored by Christ and the subject of the Lord's Prayer ('Thy Kingdom come'). Notes historical consequences: this interpretation bears on ecclesiastical government and explains why translations such as 'kingdom of priests' may obscure clerical-political implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and terminology matter for interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in translation (e.g., 'Sacerdotall Kingdome' vs 'a Kingdome of Priests' or 'Regnum Sacerdotale' vs 'Sacerdotium Regale') change the theological and institutional reading of texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translational choices can shift whether authority is read as a succession of priests or a singular high-priestly office; translators' preferences may downplay implications for Christian kings and ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Pay attention to original phrasing and parallels (e.g., St. Peter) when drawing doctrinal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy denotes proprietary, special right
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy signifies that which is God's by special, not by general, right — that which is set apart for God's especial service (e.g., the nation of the Jews), not merely anything that belongs to God in a general sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sabbath as Holy Day, Temple as Holy House, sacrifices/tithes as Holy Duties, priests/prophets/anointed kings as Holy Men, angels as Holy. The designation 'holy' implies appropriation by covenant/consent rather than mere ownership of the world generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Holy, Sacred, and Profane/Common
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacred (consecrated) refers to what is made holy by dedication to God's service; Profane commonly equals Common — the opposite of that which is set apart and public/royal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper sense: sanctification by God's appropriation (e.g., seventh day, elect endued with Spirit). Consecration by human dedication (temples, utensils, priests, victims) is also called sacred. Figuratively, people who wholly devote themselves to God may be called holy, but proper use implies propriety by covenant or consecration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of sanctity
rubrics_metrics.description: Holiness has gradations: an entire people (Israel) can be holy; within them the tribe of Levi is holier, among Levites priests holier still, and the High Priest the most holy; similarly land, city, temple, and sanctum sanctorum have ascending degrees of holiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply hierarchical distinctions when assessing the relative sanctity of persons, places, and things; consecration can be layered (public -> more special -> most exclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and functions of a Sacrament
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sacrament is a separation of some visible thing from common use and a consecration of it to God's service, serving as either a sign of admission into the Kingdom of God or for commemoration of that admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification: Sacraments of Admission (once only: circumcision in OT, baptism in NT) and Sacraments of Commemoration (reiterated: Passover, Lord's Supper). While other consecrations may be called sacraments in a broad sense, strictly speaking the sacraments that imply an oath/promise of allegiance are limited to these principal rites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacraments of admission used once; commemorations reiterated
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacraments of Admission (circumcision, baptism) are administered once because admission need occur only once; sacraments of commemoration (Passover, Lord's Supper) are repeated to remind the people of deliverance and allegiance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this functional criterion to distinguish kinds of rites and their proper frequency and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word (sermo/logos) defined as speech or discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'word' is not mere vocable (nomen or verb) but a perfect speech or discourse (sermo/logos) by which the speaker affirms, denies, commands, promises, threatens, wishes, or interrogates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the text speaks of 'word', read it as meaningful discourse with propositional content, not as an isolated lexical item. This affects interpretation of 'Word of God' passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different senses of 'Word of God' in Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Word of God' may mean (a) the words spoken by God, (b) the words concerning God (the doctrine of religion), (c) the speaker (author) of a work, or (d) the effect/thing promised by the word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context determines sense: e.g., 'Word of God' as doctrine aligns with 'theologia' or 'Word of the Gospel'; Acts and Romans cited to show doctrine-as-word. Distinguish whether a passage refers to speech-acts, doctrine content, or the promised event itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of God as doctrine (theologia/Word of the Gospel)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many New Testament uses, 'Word of God' refers to the doctrine of Christian religion, the Gospel, or the Word of Faith rather than a literal utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Acts 13:46 (Word of God as doctrine to be spoken), Acts 5:20 (words of this life meaning doctrine of the Gospel), Rom.10:8-9 (Word of Faith). Interpret 'word' passages that occur in teaching/preaching contexts as doctrinal content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of God as effect or the thing promised
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes 'Word of God' denotes the thing itself which the word promised or foretold (e.g., Joseph's 'word was come' meaning the foretold event occurred; John calling Christ the 'Word of Life' meaning the promised eternal life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sense where scriptural context points to fulfillment, outcome, or the promised reality rather than to speech or doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word of God can mean words consonant with reason and equity
rubrics_metrics.description: In some passages the 'Word of God' denotes dictates of reason and equity—even when spoken by non-prophets—because Scripture sometimes attributes such sensible counsel to God (e.g., Pharaoh Necho's words to Josiah).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a third-party or natural wisdom sense: moral or prudent counsel aligning with divine will may be treated as 'Word of God' in scriptural historiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple acceptions of 'Prophet'
rubrics_metrics.description: The name 'prophet' has several senses: prolocutor (speaker from God to man), praedictor (foreteller), and one who speaks incoherently (ecstatic/mad speech). Most frequently it denotes one to whom God speaks immediately and who relays that message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contextual clues to decide which sense applies (e.g., High Priest as prophet when enquiring in the Sanctum Sanctorum; those who teach publicly or pray for congregation may be termed prophets in some usages). Also note comparable uses among Gentiles (poets called vates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction (praediction) of future contingents is not always authentic prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Foretelling future contingents is not by itself proof of genuine prophecy; impostors and diviners may sometimes succeed by chance or deceit. Prophecy, when taken as prediction, is an extraordinary and temporary employment from God, not a constant art or vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of attributing divine authority on the basis of isolated successful predictions; consider the character, means, and continuity of the claimant and whether the event was guided by God or by imposture/fake methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes by which God speaks to extraordinary prophets (dreams and visions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For extraordinary prophets of the Old Testament (and often in the New), God commonly spoke by dreams or visions (apparitions), with many scriptural examples (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Gideon, Samuel, Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Ezekiel; also Joseph, Peter, Paul, John).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish ordinary communications (dreams/visions) from Moses' unique mode. Recognize that prophetic messages often come with signs by which presence/commandment is acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moses and sovereign prophets had a distinct, extraordinary mode
rubrics_metrics.description: To Moses (and to sovereign prophets such as the High Priest in the Tabernacle/Mercy Seat, or pious kings who inquired of God) God spoke 'mouth to mouth' or in a manner not expressible as ordinary dreams/visions; the precise manner is not detailed in Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Moses' revelations as categorically distinct from common dreams/visions; avoid reducing Sinai speech to ordinary visionary experience. The text warns against attributing human-like organs to God or equating Moses with Christ by making the mode identical to inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophets of perpetuall calling: supreme vs subordinate and their sources of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophets by perpetuity include supreme (Moses, High Priest, some pious kings) and subordinate (others). Subordinate prophets' speaking was often derived from the Spirit as inclination/disposition to obey rather than a substantial infusion of divine nature; their prophecy was subordinate to supreme prophetic authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scriptural instances (Numbers 11:70, examples of the seventy elders) to show that the Spirit in such cases denotes a disposition/grace derived from the supreme prophet rather than possession of divine essence. Evaluate prophetic claims in light of their relationship to established prophetic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking by the Spirit often denotes moral/intellectual inclination, not literal indwelling of deity
rubrics_metrics.description: When Scripture says one 'speaks by the Spirit,' it commonly means speaking according to God's will—an inclination/mind/disposition given as grace—rather than the substantial indwelling of the Divine nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this interpretive principle to avoid conflating inspired virtue or cooperative grace with ontological divinity; examples include the seventy elders and David's anointing where 'spirit' signifies gift/grace to assist governance, not Godhead.

rubrics_metrics.name: God sometimes revealed will by lots
rubrics_metrics.description: God declared his will by the outcome of lots in various Old Testament instances (e.g., Saul's lots revealing Jonathan's fault; Joshua casting lots to divide Canaan; discovering Achan's crime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize lots as a legitimate scriptural medium of divine decision mediated through authorized persons; evaluate such cases as institutional practices rather than mere chance.
